headline: Hot PPI couldn't buy the October hike back: wholesale prices ran +1.3% — the biggest jump since March 2022 — and the market still faded October to ~29%, because the AI risk-off owned the tape. The 10-year collapsed ~27bp off the CPI-day spike to a three-week low, the dollar fell against every G10 currency except the aussie, gold reclaimed ~$4,150+, and the franc — not the yen — was the haven that finally showed up. Warsh speaks 10:30pm CT, the last Fed voice before Saturday's blackout.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: Wholesale prices jumped 1.3% — more than double what was expected, the hottest since March 2022 — and the market shrugged: October hike odds fell to ~29%, the 10-year collapsed ~27bp, and the dollar faded to ~102.05.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: Wholesale prices — what businesses charge each other, the factory-gate version of inflation — rose 1.3% in a single month, the fastest since March 2022. Energy did roughly half the work: gasoline alone jumped 20.3%.
What happened: The consensus expected 0.6%. It printed 1.3% — more than double the forecast. Core (stripping out food and energy) ran 0.7% vs 0.3% expected. Thread: this morning's edition said Bowman and Daly had talked the October hike down to ~31.6% and that PPI was the next verdict. The verdict came back hot — and didn't matter.
What it means and why: The textbook chain says hot inflation → more pressure on the Fed → higher hike odds → higher yields → stronger dollar. Today the chain broke at the first link. The market chose the fear tape over the inflation tape: AI-debt stress (Nasdaq's fourth straight down day, CoreWeave bonds above 16%) sent money into Treasuries for safety, and buying Treasuries pushes their yields DOWN — the 10-year fell ~27bp to ~5.05-5.10%, a three-week low. October pricing slipped to ~29%. The beginner's lesson: the number describes the economy; the market move comes from what the market does with it — and today fear out-shouted inflation. December (~90%+) never blinked, and MarketWatch's read was blunt: hot PPI is 'still not turning market in favor of an October rate hike.'
What it indicates for the dollar: Softer. The chain ran in reverse — risk-off → safety buying of Treasuries → lower yields → a smaller rate advantage for holding dollars → DXY faded to ~102.03-102.07. The reusable question: when hot data and fear collide, which tape is running the market?
chapters.fx: What to watch: Warsh speaks 10:30pm CT — the last Fed voice before Saturday's Oct 17 blackout (Hammack spoke 3:30pm CT; no verified readout had surfaced by NY close — her Monday 'rates need to move higher' stance is already priced). Friday 7:30am CT: import prices + housing starts; 8:15am CT: industrial production. September PCE lands Oct 29, after the meeting.

scenarios.base: October stays ~25-30% into the blackout; the meeting is priced as a hold and DXY chops 101.8-102.5.
scenarios.bear: A patient Warsh plus soft Friday data — October falls toward ~15% and DXY retests 101.5.
scenarios.bull: Warsh re-arms the hike — October back toward ~45% and DXY retests 102.75.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro rode the dollar fade to ~1.12 (+0.5%) even as its own data disappointed — eurozone factory output missed and France's inflation confirmed the energy overshoot.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The euro rose about half a percent against the dollar to ~1.1216, fully recovering the CPI-day selloff — even though Europe's own numbers were soft.
What happened: Eurozone industrial production fell 0.5% in August vs flat expected (July revised deeper too). France's final September CPI confirmed the overshoot: 3.4% y/y, the highest since January 2024, with energy doing the work. Thread: this morning's edition said the pair trades the Fed leg, not the ECB leg.
What it means and why: Neither European print moved the pair — and that's the point. EUR/USD is a ratio: it rises when the dollar falls even if nothing good happened in Europe. This week's euro is a dollar story with a fiscal overhang (the €100B+ war-driven fossil import bill hanging over winter). The ECB leg is the steady one — Simkus talking about possible tightening, October 29 hike barely priced at ~12%.
What it indicates for the euro: Higher vs the dollar, but on borrowed strength — it's the dollar fading, not the euro shining. The chain: US yields fell → the dollar weakened broadly → EUR/USD rose mechanically. The reusable question: which leg is moving the pair — the Fed leg or the ECB leg?

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: Sterling rode the dollar fade to ~1.324 (+0.4%) as a Reuters poll showed 54 of 63 economists expect the November hike — while Pill said it 'need not be the start of a long series.'
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The pound rose to ~1.3230-1.3242, recovering from the post-CPI low of 1.3137, as a poll confirmed the November rate hike is the consensus view.
What happened: 54 of 63 economists surveyed expect +25bp to 4.00% at the November 5 meeting. But no majority expects another hike after that — 30 of 61 see one more in Q1 2027, while markets price four by September 2027. Pill, speaking on day two, said a hike 'need not be the start of a long series,' while warning that catch-up wage dynamics need 'a prolonged period of restriction.' Thread: this morning said the GDP beat covered the growth leg of the November case while Pill capped the 2027 path.
What it means and why: A rate hike normally supports a currency — higher rates → higher yields → money flows in. But it's the PATH that matters, not the single hike: November is ~86% priced, so it's already in the price. Pill is hawkish on inflation but dovish on how far they'll go, and the economists sit between Pill and the market. The gap between 'one hike' and 'four hikes' is where sterling's next move lives.
What it indicates for the pound: Supported near-term by the near-certain November hike, capped beyond it by the path debate. The chain: priced hike = no surprise = no new fuel; a hawkish surprise on the path (or soft US data) is what extends the move. The reusable question: is the market pricing the hike or the path?

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: USD/JPY faded to ~157.7 with the 10-year as Koeda warned against getting 'overly cautious' on hikes — but the franc, not the yen, was Thursday's haven.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The yen strengthened a touch — USD/JPY slipped ~0.2% to ~157.6-157.9 — moving with falling US yields, while a Bank of Japan board member talked tough on future hikes.
What happened: The pair faded as the 10-year fell to its three-week low — USD/JPY still breathes with the US yield leg. Koeda said the BoJ should not get 'overly cautious' on rate hikes and put the neutral rate 'considerably above 1%,' citing upside inflation risks from AI demand, Middle East tensions, and the weak yen feeding raw-material costs. Thread: this morning said the BoJ side is frozen in the December-not-October shape and that the haven bid still isn't independent.
What it means and why: The yen has two engines — the rate gap and fear. Engine one: when US yields fall, the US-Japan rate gap narrows, and the yen rises (less reason to borrow cheap yen and park it in high-yielding dollars). Engine two: in a panic, money buys yen as a haven. Koeda keeps December (>80%) alive with October (~9%) unchanged — hawkish noise, no near-term action. And the haven lesson from today: the franc (+0.59%) beat the yen (+0.34%) on the same risk-off tape — when the fear is financial (AI debt) rather than geopolitical, Europe's haven out-bids Japan's.
What it indicates for the yen: Mildly supportive — both engines pointed the same way, softly. The chain: lower US yields → narrower rate gap → yen up; fear bid → yen up, but second to the franc. The reusable question: is the yen moving on the rate gap or on fear?

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The haven finally showed up: USD/CHF fell ~0.57% to ~0.83 — Thursday's best G10 move against the dollar — while soft Swiss PPI kept December cut risk on the table.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The franc woke up. USD/CHF dropped to ~0.831 — the strongest G10 move against the dollar on the board — as fear bid Europe's haven.
What happened: The franc outperformed the yen on the same risk-off tape (CHF/JPY +0.36%) — the haven bid picked Europe over Japan. Switzerland's own print was soft: PPI +0.3% m/m vs 0.6% expected (official BFS data), so pipeline price pressures stay tame. Thread: this morning's edition said the franc slept through a genuine risk-off night and only moves on a verified shock or de-escalation.
What it means and why: That thesis just broke — and the pattern is instructive. When the fear is about credit and AI debt (CoreWeave bonds above 16%), the haven flow goes franc first, gold second, yen third. The soft PPI keeps December SNB cut risk alive, but with rates pinned at 0.00% there's barely anything left to cut — and a central bank that can't cut much further is itself franc-supportive, because the yield disadvantage can't widen.
What it indicates for the franc: Supportive into the weekend — fear bid plus no dovish surprise. The chain: credit fear → safety demand for francs → USD/CHF down; soft domestic inflation = no reason for the SNB to surprise either way. The reusable question: what kind of fear is it — financial fear (franc's game) or geopolitical fear (yen's game)?

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The aussie was the only G10 currency to fall against the dollar Thursday (-0.48% to ~0.694): a jobs miss plus a risk-off tape is the worst possible combination for a risk proxy.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The Australian dollar fell ~0.5% to ~0.6939 — the lone loser among G10 currencies on a day every other one gained on the dollar.
What happened: September jobs missed badly: -39,300 vs +20,000 expected, and unemployment jumped to 4.7% — a five-year high, above the RBA's own 4.5% forecast for Q4. Thread: this morning said the miss broke the improving-AUD shape and pushed the $0.70 test further away.
What it means and why: Think of the aussie as a risk proxy — it rises when the world feels brave and falls when it feels scared. A jobs miss plus a risk-off tape (Nasdaq's fourth straight down day, Asian equities routed overnight) is the worst possible combination: the domestic story breaks (bad jobs = less pressure on the RBA to hike — November odds pared from ~33%) at the exact moment the global mood punishes risk. The record shorts (-98,588, roughly the 2nd percentile) mean a squeeze is loaded — a lot of traders betting against the aussie who'd have to buy it back in a hurry — but it now needs two things: soft US data and an RBA willing to hike through labor-market slack.
What it indicates for the aussie: Pressured — both legs (domestic miss, global fear) point down. The chain: weak jobs → less RBA hike pressure → lower expected yields → less reason to hold AUD; plus risk-off → risk proxies sold. The reusable question: does the RBA hike through the slack or blink?

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The tug-of-war's legs pushed the same way for once: the EIA confirmed a -8.6M-barrel draw and WTI rallied +2.7% while the dollar leg faded — the loonie firmed gently to ~1.42.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The loonie firmed to ~1.42 (-0.18% on USD/CAD) as its two drivers — oil and the US dollar — both pointed its way.
What happened: The EIA confirmed the big API draw: crude stocks fell 8.6M barrels (vs +0.2M expected) to 415.6M, 3% below the five-year average; total commercial petroleum stocks fell 13.4M. December WTI rallied 2.7% to $96.42 while December Brent sat ~$106.10 little changed — the Brent-WTI spread compressed to ~$9.7 from ~$10.5. Canada's factory sales beat (+1.5% vs 1.1%) but volumes were flat — prices did all the work, which is inflation, not growth. Thread: this morning said both tug-of-war legs eased in tandem and the 1.41-1.43 chop holds until one side wins.
What it means and why: Canada sells oil to the world, so tight physical supply (a big draw = less oil sitting in tanks) supports the loonie — the gap decides direction, oil decides magnitude. The spread is the tell: Brent carries the freight-and-war premium, WTI doesn't. When the spread compresses on shadow-fleet sanctions-easing talk, the fear premium is leaking out of Brent — Phil Flynn's read is that easing would be 'more negative for Brent than WTI' because the elevated freight cost lives in Brent's price.
What it indicates for the loonie: Gently supportive — tight oil plus a soft dollar is the friendly combination. The chain: big draw → tighter physical market → higher WTI → better Canadian terms of trade → CAD bid; plus dollar fade → USD/CAD down. The line in the sand is the 52-week high at 1.4299. The reusable question: which leg wins the tug-of-war — the oil bid or the dollar?

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi drifted +0.2% to ~0.562 on the dollar fade while RBNZ's Conway confirmed the two-way bet: October 28 is 'wide open,' but the direction is 'most likely up.'
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The New Zealand dollar added ~0.2% to ~0.5616 on the dollar fade, still hovering just above its 52-week low of 0.5580.
What happened: RBNZ chief economist Paul Conway, speaking on the IMF sidelines in Bangkok, said the October 28 decision is 'wide open' — policymakers want the flexibility to hold or hike 25bp — but the direction of the OCR is 'most likely up.' His reasoning: oil gains plus a weaker NZD are adding near-term inflation pressure, though the board still expects inflation back inside the 1-3% band next year. Thread: this morning framed October 28 as a genuine two-way bet (~50% priced) with NZ CPI on Oct 21 as the settler.
What it means and why: A central bank leaning hawkish normally supports its currency — expected hikes → higher expected yields → money flows in. But 'wide open' means the market can't price it yet, so the currency drifts instead of trending. Conway validated the two-way framing and leaned it hawkish at the margin. Tonight's BusinessNZ PMI and food prices are texture; the CPI on Oct 21 is the verdict.
What it indicates for the kiwi: Stuck near the lows until the data decides. The chain: hot Oct 21 CPI → hike gets priced → NZD re-rates up; soft CPI → hold → NZD stays heavy. The reusable question: what does the CPI say about October 28?

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: The EIA confirmed the draw (-8.6M barrels): WTI rallied +2.7% to $96.42 while Brent lagged — the spread compressed to ~$9.7 as the freight premium, not demand, is what's priced.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: The official EIA report confirmed the huge draw the API had flagged — US crude stocks fell 8.6M barrels — and WTI rallied 2.7% to $96.42 while Brent barely moved.
What happened: Crude -8.6M barrels vs +0.2M expected, to 415.6M — 3% below the five-year average. Gasoline built 3.5M, distillates drew 2.5M (12% below seasonal norms), total commercial stocks -13.4M. December Brent sat ~$106.10 little changed, so the Brent-WTI spread compressed from ~$10.5 to ~$9.7. Thread: this morning said Brent $104-108 holds until a verified shock or ceasefire, the API draw was ignored, and the EIA was the confirmation test.
What it means and why: A draw means physical tightness — less oil in tanks than the market expected — which is bullish on its own. But Brent lagging tells the deeper story: the war premium lives in Brent as a freight-and-shipping cost, not in WTI. Talk of easing shadow-fleet tanker sanctions (a consideration, not an action) leaked some of that premium out — easing would be 'more negative for Brent than WTI,' as Phil Flynn put it, because the elevated freight cost is priced into Brent. Fresh US sanctions on Iran (16 individuals, 10 entities) and CNN's report of new strike plans including a MOAB option (planning, not an order) kept the escalatory lane open. The spread is the gauge: toward $15 = Hormuz risk back in force; toward $5 = the premium is gone.
What it indicates for oil: Range intact — physical tightness re-bid WTI and unwound part of Brent's freight premium, but didn't break $104-108. The market still needs a verified shock or a ceasefire to leave the range. The reusable question: is the spread pricing shipping risk or demand?

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: The anti-dollar bid re-armed: gold ran to ~$4,150-4,175 (+1.5%+, futures $4,181 +1.8%) as the rate leg collapsed — the haven that works when FX havens hesitate.
chapters.meaning:
What this was: Gold's bounce became a rally — spot ~$4,150-4,175, futures +1.79% to $4,181.30 — as falling yields re-armed the anti-dollar bid.
What happened: Yesterday's hot CPI had knocked gold down 1.66% to $4,107.90 (the rate leg winning). Today's collapse in the 10-year to its three-week low flipped it: the rate leg eased, and gold ripped back. Thread: this morning called CPI day the both-engines moment and said the overnight ease had re-armed the bid.
What it means and why: Gold runs on two engines, and both fired today. Engine one — real yields: gold pays nothing, so it competes with yield; when yields fall, holding gold gets cheaper and it rallies. Engine two — fear: AI-debt stress, crypto liquidations near $1B, and the defensive rotation (healthcare +2.6%, staples +1% while the Nasdaq fell a fourth straight day) all bid the ultimate no-counterparty asset. The comparison tells the story: gold +1.8% vs franc +0.59% vs yen +0.34% — gold is the haven that works when FX havens hesitate.
What it indicates for gold: Re-armed but capped — the 10-year (~5.05-5.10%) is the cap to watch. The chain: yields down → gold's competition fades → gold up; fear up → haven demand → gold up. If Friday's data collapses the October repricing, $4,300 comes back into view; a hawkish Warsh re-fires it and gold slides back toward $4,000. The reusable question: which engine is running — rates or fear?
